summary: Describes the certificate policy for the PKI used to attest to holdings of Internet number resources. Each organization that hands out addresses or AS numbers issues a certificate reflecting that, so holders can prove who currently holds what. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: This document sets out the rules for the certificate system used by the Resource Public Key Infrastructure. The certificates do not say who an organisation is; they say which IP addresses and AS numbers that organisation currently holds, so anyone can check the claim.

questions: what is the rpki certificate policy
how often must rpki crls be checked
subtitle: The rules that govern how certificates are issued in the system that proves who holds IP addresses and AS numbers.

tldr.problem: The Resource Public Key Infrastructure needs a written policy for how certificates are issued, renewed, revoked and published, so that a holder of an IP address or AS number can prove it is the current holder.
tldr.mechanism: The document is a certificate policy built on the RFC 3647 template: it names the participants, the permitted uses of the certificates, the identity checks, the certificate life cycle, the repository rules and the operational controls, leaving the detailed practice to each authority's own statement.
tldr.outcome: Published as Best Current Practice 173 in February 2012, it is the policy that the rest of the RPKI standards are written against.

facts.label: CRL checks by relying parties
facts.value: At least daily, at most 8-12 times per day

today: RFC 6484 is Best Current Practice 173, published in February 2012. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it remains the certificate policy that the other RPKI documents are written against.

sections.title: What This Policy Is For
sections.content:
The RPKI is a public key infrastructure used to attest to holdings of Internet Number Resources, meaning IP addresses and Autonomous System numbers. An organisation that hands out such resources to another organisation MAY, in parallel, issue a public key certificate that reflects the handover. Those certificates let anyone verify that the resources named in the certificate were distributed to the holder of the matching private key, and that this organisation is the current holder of them.

The distinguishing feature of this PKI is that it does not claim to identify an INR holder from the subject name in the certificate. Each certificate exists so that an entity can assert, in a verifiable way, that it currently holds a resource, based on the records of the organisation responsible for that resource. Verification rests on two things: the ability of the entity to sign data that verifies under the public key in the certificate, and the validation of that certificate within this PKI.

The infrastructure is designed only for validating claims about current holdings. That includes certificates issued to support the operation of the infrastructure itself, for example for the integrity and access control of the repository system, and such transitive uses are permitted. Using the certificates and CRLs for any other purpose violates this policy, and relying parties SHOULD reject certificates presented for such uses.

The document follows the template in RFC 3647. Several template sections are omitted because they do not apply to this PKI, but the section numbering is kept so that the two can be compared, and each omitted section is to be read as "No stipulation".
sections.plainLanguage: The certificates in this system do not identify a company. They let a company say "these addresses are mine" and let others check that the saying is true.

sections.title: Who Takes Part
sections.content:
The structure of the RPKI matches the way number resources are allocated. IANA allocates resources to the Regional Internet Registries, to others, and for special purposes. The RIRs in turn manage the allocation of resources to end users, Internet Service Providers and others.

The organisations that distribute IP addresses and AS numbers, namely IANA, the RIRs, NIRs and ISPs, act as certification authorities in this PKI. Organisations that do not distribute resources but hold them also act as CAs when they create end-entity certificates. The PKI does not need a registration authority function separate from the CA function: the same entity that operates as CA must provide the RA function, because it already has a formal relationship with each organisation to which it distributes resources and already assumes responsibility for that distribution.

The subscribers are the organisations receiving the distributions: RIRs, NIRs, ISPs and others. Any of them may have received resources from more than one source over time, which is true even for RIRs, since they take part in inter-registry exchanges of address space. Relying parties are the entities or individuals who act in reliance on the certificates or on RPKI signed objects; they need not be subscribers themselves. Every organisation acting as CA is responsible for populating the distributed repository with the certificates, CRLs and signed objects it issues, either through its own publication point or by outsourcing that function.
sections.plainLanguage: The people who give out addresses are the certificate authorities here. They pass a certificate down the same chain they use to pass the addresses, so the chain of certificates mirrors the chain of allocations.

sections.title: What the Certificates May Be Used For
sections.content:
The certificates issued under this hierarchy are for authorization in support of validating claims of current holdings. Additional uses consistent with that goal are permitted, for example certificates issued to support integrity and access control for the repository system. Any other use is prohibited, and relying parties SHOULD reject a certificate presented for such a use.

Naming follows the same logic. The distinguished name for every CA and end entity consists of a single common name generated by the issuer, and the serial number attribute MAY be included to tell successive certificates for the same entity apart. The subject name SHOULD NOT be meaningful, because the name is not intended to convey the identity of the subject to relying parties. Anonymity is not a function of this PKI, so although names may appear random, no explicit support for it is provided.

There is no guarantee that subject names are globally unique. Each CA certifies names that MUST be unique among the certificates it issues, and names SHOULD be built so that two entities are unlikely to be assigned the same one. The RPKI Certificate Profile gives an example of how to generate meaningless names that make collisions unlikely. The rules for interpreting name forms are "None".
sections.plainLanguage: These certificates may only be used to check who holds a resource. They are not identity certificates, so the name inside them carries no meaning and may even look random.

sections.title: Repositories and Publication
sections.content:
Certificates, CRLs and RPKI signed objects intended for public consumption MUST be available for download by all relying parties, so that they can validate the data. That motivates a robust, distributed repository system. Each CA MUST maintain a publicly accessible online repository and publish its RPKI signed objects through it in the manner described in "A Profile for Resource Certificate Repository Structure" (RFC 6481), and the collection of repositories is the RPKI distributed repository system. Publishing may be outsourced to another organisation.

Each CA MUST publish the certificates, CRLs and RPKI signed objects it issues that are intended for public consumption. It SHOULD create and publish a Certification Practice Statement, a document describing the practices that the CA employs when issuing certificates, whenever it issues certificates to entities outside its own administrative domain. Publication means the affected entities must be able to get a copy and to tell when it changes.

The timing rules are also stated. Each CA's practice statement must say how long it takes to publish a certificate after issuing it, and how long it takes to publish a CRL with an entry for a revoked certificate after revoking it. Expired and revoked certificates SHOULD be removed from the repository, and each CA MUST publish its next CRL before the nextUpdate value carried in the previous one.

Repository access controls are required to stop unauthorised people adding, changing or deleting entries. A CA or repository operator MUST NOT deliberately limit read access to its practice statement, certificates, CRLs or signed objects, because that data is meant to be public.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything is published where anyone can fetch it, because that is how the checking works. The only thing that is locked down is who may put things in or take them out.

sections.title: Identifying the Holder
sections.content:
Every CA must require each subject to prove possession of the private key matching the public key in the certificate before the certificate is issued. How that proof is obtained is left to each CA, which must describe it in its practice statement.

The organisation behind a certificate must be authenticated in the way the CA already authenticates organisations that receive resources, because the CA's own records of who holds what are the basis for the certificate. At least one individual must be identified as a representative of each organisation that holds resources, and the CA must verify that a person claiming to represent an organisation is authorised to do so in this context. These procedures are described in the practice statement, and relying parties may expect each CA to use procedures commensurate with those it already uses as a registry or ISP.

The Resource PKI SHOULD NOT be used to authenticate the identity of an organisation. Its job is to bind subscribers to the resources they hold, so the application procedures need not verify legal organisation names. A CA MUST NOT put non-verified subscriber data into the certificates it issues, with the exception of Subject Information Access extensions. Re-key and revocation requests have their own authentication rules: the requester must be the legitimate holder, and proof of possession of the new private key is required even when a re-key follows a revocation. The PKI is neither intended nor designed to interoperate with any other PKI.
sections.plainLanguage: Before issuing a certificate, the authority checks that the requester really holds the key it is asking for, and that it is the organisation the authority's own records say holds the addresses. It does not check the organisation's legal identity.

sections.title: Renewal, Re-Key, Modification and Revocation
sections.content:
Renewal replaces a certificate before it expires. Only the validity dates and the serial number change; the public key and all other information stay the same. It must be processed when the certificate expires or when the subscriber asks, and the subscriber is responsible for renewing in time. If the CA starts the process because of the expiry date it MUST notify the holder in advance. The validity of the new certificate SHOULD overlap the old one, and it is RECOMMENDED that the renewed certificate be issued and published at least 1 week before the certificate it replaces expires.

Re-key replaces the key as well as the certificate. It SHOULD be performed only when required, either because of knowledge or suspicion that the private key has been compromised or lost, or because the cryptographic lifetime of the key pair has ended. A re-key has dramatic consequences, because every certificate issued by the re-keyed entity has to be reissued, so it must be done in a way that preserves the ability of relying parties to validate certificates whose path includes that entity. CA key rollover MUST follow the procedures in RFC 6489.

Modification covers changes to the resource holdings described in the RFC 3779 extensions and to the Subject Information Access extension. When no holdings are removed, the new certificate keeps the same public key and expiry date, and revoking the old one is not required. When holdings are removed, the old certificate MUST be revoked and a new one issued.

A certificate MUST be revoked if there is reason to believe the subscriber's private key has been compromised, and MAY be revoked to invalidate an object signed with that key. If resources are only being added, the old certificate need not be revoked, because a new certificate can carry both the old and the new resources and the old key. A relying party MUST acquire and check the most recent scheduled CRL from the issuer whenever it validates a certificate. The CRL frequency is set by each CA and stated in its practice statement, and each CRL carries the nextUpdate value at which a new one is due. This PKI makes no provision for OCSP or SCVP, because those are not designed for bulk checking at this scale: relying parties MUST check for new CRLs at least daily, and it is RECOMMENDED that they do so several times per day but no more than 8 to 12 times per day.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four things you can do to a certificate: renew it with the same key, replace the key, change what addresses it covers, or cancel it. Every one of those steps has rules, and everyone who checks the certificates has to fetch the list of cancelled ones.

sections.title: Controls on the Authorities
sections.content:
Each CA must maintain physical security controls for its operation that are commensurate with those it uses when managing resource distribution, and must describe them in its practice statement. The topics a practice statement may cover include site location and construction, physical access, power and air conditioning, water exposure, fire prevention, media storage, waste disposal and off-site backup.

Procedural controls cover the trusted roles in the organisation, how many people are needed for each task, how each role is identified and authenticated, and which roles require separation of duties. Personnel controls and audit logging procedures follow: the events that are recorded, how often the log is processed, how long it is kept, how it is protected, and how it is backed up. Vulnerability assessments are part of the logging requirements.

On the technical side, the algorithms and key sizes used in the RPKI are set out in RFC 6485, and the key usage purposes are set in the RPKI Certificate Profile. Each subscriber is responsible for checking the quality of its own key pair, and a CA is responsible only when it generated the key on the subscriber's behalf. Each CA MUST back up its private keys securely, because losing the use of a CA key has adverse operational consequences. No private key escrow procedures are required for the RPKI.
sections.plainLanguage: The authorities that issue these certificates have to run their key rooms properly: physical security, clear roles, logs that are kept, and backups of the keys they would be lost without.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A certificate policy is a named set of rules indicating the applicability of a certificate to a particular community or class of applications with common security requirements, and a relying party may use it to decide whether a certificate and its binding are trustworthy enough for a given application. Separate practice statements cover the factors that determine how far that trust goes: the practices the CA uses to authenticate the subject, its operating policy and procedures and technical security controls, the scope of the subscriber's responsibilities such as protecting the private key, and the stated responsibilities and liability terms of the CA.

One risk follows from names not being unique across the RPKI: two CAs may issue certificates and CRLs under the same issuer name. Path validation that follows the resource certification path validation algorithm in RFC 6487 verifies that the same key was used to sign both the resource certificate and the matching CRL, so a name collision does not change the result. The basic X.509 path validation algorithm assumes name uniqueness, and using it could result in a revoked certificate being accepted as valid, or a valid certificate being rejected as revoked. Relying parties must make sure their software checks that the same key signed the certificate and its CRL.
sections.plainLanguage: Two different authorities can end up with the same name, so the checking software has to compare keys rather than names when it matches a certificate to its list of cancelled ones.

viz.caption: FOUR DEFINING PROPERTIES OF THE RPKI

items.title: Not an identity system
items.text: The subject name carries no meaning and need not be unique across the PKI.

items.title: Proof of possession
items.text: A subscriber must show it holds the private key before a certificate is issued.

items.title: Public repository
items.text: Certificates and CRLs are published for anyone to download.

items.title: No interoperation
items.text: This PKI is neither intended nor designed to work with any other PKI.
